In the development of academic CubeSat-based space missions, it is common to skip or rush many practices of the Systems Engineering Process due to time and cost constraints, which may lead to issues later on in the mission and failures.

With the purpose of supporting these analyses, this article introduces a workflow based on a Cyber-Physical abstraction of CubeSat mission operation scenarios, which uses architectural models based on SysML Class Diagrams and automatic model transformation to support the simulation of these operational scenarios in an open source Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) tool.

One of the most important analyses in the initial design phase of the satellite mission involves the balance of power and data budget. The modeling and simulation of the in-orbit operational behavior of the satellite with power and data budget analyses is a fundamental step in this stage.

Simulating the operations scenarios that express the power consumption and data generation of the CubeSat platform itself and on board payloads allows for the verification of mission requirements, evidencing inconsistencies between what is expected from the mission in terms of data acquisition [4].

Based on physical and logical models, which represent the major cyberphysical elements involved in both ground and space segments concerning the operation of the CubeSat mission, a tool was developed, called C2F, to automatically generate code used as an input for a satellite simulator called ForPlan [4].

The main contributions introduced in this paper are 1) the structured mission architecture model defining operations scenarios, along with 2) the C2F plugin to automatically transform this model into a configuration script for the ForPlan simulator.

The user then analyses the results of the simulation outputs, such as battery capacity and data usage graphs, to see if the operations requirements are met, or if they should proceed to another iteration changing the model parameters for another operations scenario simulation. When the requirements are met, the user may use these results to drive further design implementations.

ForPlan creates a Low-Earth Orbit space environment, simulating the behavior of a spacecraft from an operational perspective along the orbit, taking into account the operation of each individual equipment in terms of electrical power consumption and data volume generation, and the interaction of the satellite with the Sun (electrical power generation) and with the associated ground stations (data downlink).

To define a mission and prepare it for simulation on ForPlan, users (who will run a simulation using the software) must write a Julia language configuration script where all of the simulation parameters are declared.

The Equipment Operation Functions are functions that get evaluated at each iteration step for each individual equipment, and based on parameters and internal conditions defined in them, describe when the equipment will be turned on/off, how much power it will consume and how much data it will generate.

1) AlwaysOn - Equipment is always turned on in a constant state.

2) OnGroundStation - Equipment is turned on whenever above the ground stations listed as parameters.

3) TimedOp - Equipment is periodically turned on. Parameters define on-time and off-time.

4) RoiOP - Equipment is turned on whenever above regions of interest (ROI).

In order to overcome this problem, we have defined a set of rules (well-formed constraints) in the context of the Class Diagram language, specifying interpretable models for later processing steps in the approach.
Data Packages separate the Class Instances into different types, defining how they will be transformed into the script.

The users then can create an "instance" class diagram MAM based on this abstract class diagram and define their own mission by creating class instances (instantiating data packages) for their specific mission and assign values to the properties according to the respective parameters for their mission, preparing the architecture model to be transformed into the ForPlan simulator input script.
C2F traverses the model elements of the MAM in accordance with the predefined rules overviewed in Section II and generates Julia code based on the retrieved attributes.

C2F is integrated into Capella via a context menu item that appears when right-clicking on a Capella model file with a Class Diagram and executes the model transformation, outputting the Julia script into the destination src-gen folder inside the project directory.

This workflow was applied for the NanosatC-Br2 mission, where the resulting model was used to generate simulations for operations scenarios to be used in discussions among the stakeholders to reach a viable operation scenario.

This model is the final version of a number of iterations of generating a model, using C2F to generate the simulation input script, simulating the defined scenario, and analyzing the simulation results.

These graphs show the battery charge levels and mass memory for an operation scenario of NanosatC-Br2 considering a time-based operation for two of the payloads (SMDH and SDATF) and a ROI-based operation for the SLP payload and on-board magnetometer.

From these graphs, we can infer that the power and data balances are stable, i.e. the satellite is capable of charging the batteries for the amount used each orbit, and download the generated mission data.
for this perspective, that this is a valid operation scenario. The scenario was then used to drive the implementations for the flight software.

In addition, an example application for the NanosatC-Br2 mission was demonstrated. The resulting feasible operations scenario was used to drive further implementations in the on-board software development.

In order to apply this workflow for other satellite simulators, the user would have to first change the MAM to fit the required inputs for the new simulator, and then change the C2F tool to meet the way the new simulator should be configured.

By using the MAM and automatically generating the input configuration script, the user is no longer required to understand how the simulator source code works, and does not have to manually code the configurations for each scenario, permitting a straightforward use of the simulator.
Also, it is much more practical and faster to change scenario parameters in the model than manually in the configuration script, facilitating the work involved.

For future work, we plan to define a process to model userdefined Equipment Operation Functions and have a method in C2F to automatically generate the ForPlan function for that, in order to extend the current four pre-defined functions.
